sessions.title: EPISTEMOLOGY — PERCEPTION AS THE SOLE MEANS OF VALID KNOWLEDGE (pramāṇa)

technical.before: Pratyakṣaika-pramāṇavāda: perception alone is a means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa); everything else in the system follows logically from this. ✅ Chatterjee and Datta: "The entire philosophy of the Cārvākas may be said to depend logically on their epistemology." ✅ The Cārvāka's test for pramāṇa-hood: knowledge "about which we can have no doubt" and "which must be true to reality". ✅ Both external and internal perception are admitted; consciousness is perceived, an immaterial soul is not. ✅ Cārvāka denies the inference from consciousness to a soul, not consciousness itself. ✅ "Truth is not an unfailing character of all inferences; it is only an accident, and a separable one." ⚠️ Distinguish laukika (corrigible, practical) from pāramārthika (uncheckable, transcendental) inference; the second is the real target. ✅ Verbal testimony (śabda) in five steps: words heard are perceived → what they mean is unperceived → acceptance runs through a reliability inference → inference is precarious → testimony is not independent. ✅ Sharma's reductio: if testimony proved invariable concomitance (vyāpti), "none would be able to infer anything by himself". ✅ The Veda is rejected as the work of "cunning priests" whose promises benefit only the officiants — an epistemic charge with a sociological edge. ⚠️ The single template that kills comparison (upamāna), postulation (arthāpatti) and non-cognition (anupalabdhi): each needs an unperceived universal. ⚠️ Sharma's charge: Cārvāka accepts perception and rejects inference from the same standpoint, lacking the saṃvṛti/paramārtha or vyāvahārika/pāramārthika distinction that saves Śūnyavāda and Advaita.
technical.after: Perception-only epistemology (pratyakṣaika-pramāṇavāda) treats perception as the sole independent means of valid knowledge and reduces inference and testimony to fallible practical reliance.

sessions.title: MOMENTARINESS, CAUSAL EFFICIENCY AND CONTINUITY

technical.before: Causal efficacy (arthakriyā) (causal efficacy / capacity to perform a function) is the Buddhist pramāṇa-school criterion of the real: sat = arthakriyā-samartha — the real is what is capable of producing an effect. ✅ Momentariness (kṣaṇikavāda) follows because whatever is causally effective must be moment-specific; a wholly permanent entity cannot explain why an effect appears now rather than always. ⚠️ This is the bridge between Buddhist epistemology and ontology: the same test that ranks svalakṣaṇa (unique particular) as ultimately real also grounds the thesis yat sat tat kṣaṇikam — whatever is real is momentary.
technical.after: Buddhist momentariness links reality to moment-specific causal efficacy and explains continuity through succession, not through a numerically identical permanent substance.

plain.before: Avyākata / avyākṛta (undeclared / unanswered) questions are questions the Buddha declines to answer in the expected metaphysical format. ✅ They include whether the world is eternal or not eternal, finite or infinite; whether the individual self (jīva) (life-principle / self) is the same as or different from the body; and whether the Tathāgata exists after death, does not exist, both, or neither.

technical.before: The questions are na arthasaṃhita (not conducive to the goal / not connected with welfare and liberation). ✅ The arrow parable in the Cūḷamālukya teaching compares the metaphysical questioner to a man shot with a poisoned arrow who refuses treatment until he learns the archer's caste, name, bow-type and arrow-fletching; he dies before treatment. ✅ The questions rest on a false presupposition: they assume a substantial self or substantial world about which the alternatives can be predicated. ⚠️ The structure resembles the loaded question “Have you stopped beating your wife?”; any direct answer concedes the presupposition. ✅ Conditioned cognition cannot settle what is framed beyond the conditions of meaningful experience and liberation-oriented practice.
technical.after: Buddhist suspension on the avyākata questions is therapeutic and logical: it blocks ill-formed metaphysical alternatives while directing inquiry toward dependent origination and liberation.

plain.after: Primordial nature (prakṛti) is the unmanifest material root constituted by the three guṇas, whose changing proportions explain psychological and cosmic diversity.

technical.before: Primordial material nature (prakṛti) is the unmanifest, unconscious, primordial material principle from which the entire objective and psycho-physical world evolves. ✅ It is also called unmanifest material root (pradhāna) (chief principle) because it is the primary material basis of all empirical manifestation. ✅ It is called unmanifest nature (avyakta) (unmanifest) because in its primordial condition it is not yet differentiated into manifest principles (tattvas). ✅ It is not a created entity; it is the ultimate material cause of the world within Sāṃkhya's dualist ontology. ⚠️ In exam language, Primordial material nature (prakṛti) is not merely "matter" in the modern physicalist sense; it includes the roots of intellect, ego, mind, senses, subtle elements and gross elements.
technical.after: Sāṃkhya infers prakṛti as an uncreated, unconscious and all-inclusive material cause containing the roots of intellect, mind, senses and physical elements.

sessions.title: BONDAGE, DISCRIMINATIVE KNOWLEDGE AND ISOLATION (kaivalya)

technical.before: Bondage in Sāṃkhya is aviveka, non-discrimination between Conscious witness (puruṣa) and Primordial material nature (prakṛti). ✅ Determinative intellect (buddhi) reflects consciousness, and this reflection creates false identification. ✅ The self then appears as agent, enjoyer, sufferer and knower in the empirical sense. ⚠️ Bondage is not real alteration in Conscious witness (puruṣa) but mistaken identification through reflected consciousness.
technical.after: Sāṃkhya bondage is beginningless misidentification between witness-consciousness and prakṛti's products; discriminative knowledge ends appropriation and yields kaivalya.

answer_line.before: Liberation is discriminative knowledge (viveka-jñāna), discriminative knowledge that "I am not Primordial material nature (prakṛti)." ✅ When the distinction between witness-consciousness and guṇic evolutes becomes steady, false identification ends. ✅ This state is isolation (kaivalya), the aloneness or isolation of Conscious witness (puruṣa). ⚠️ Isolation (kaivalya) is not merger; it is disentanglement.
answer_line.after: Sāṃkhya liberation is isolation through knowledge, not union: puruṣa ceases to identify with prakṛti once their radical difference is discriminatively known.

sessions.title: VEDĀNTIC AND VIVEKANANDAN PLURALISM

plain.before: "Ekaṃ sad viprā bahudhā vadanti" — Ṛgveda 1.164.46, from the asya vāmasya riddle-hymn ascribed to Dīrghatamas — "the one existent, the wise speak of in many ways". ⚠️ Attribution discipline (examiner-visible): (i) cite the reference as RV 1.164.46, not vaguely as "the Vedas"; (ii) the verse's own context is the naming of deities — it lists Indra, Mitra, Varuṇa, Agni, the celestial Garutmān, Yama and Mātariśvan as names of "the one existent" — so its native subject is the unity of the Vedic pantheon, not the unity of the world's religions; (iii) its extension into a charter of inter-religious pluralism is a nineteenth- and twentieth-century development (Vivekananda, Radhakrishnan, Gandhi) and must be argued for, not asserted by citation; (iv) common transliteration variants (ekaṃ sat vipra bahudhā vadanti) are acceptable, but keep one form consistently. ✅ Used with that discipline it remains the strongest single Indian text for the pluralist case — precisely because it distinguishes one referent from many names. ✅ Vivekananda — Universal Religion: all religions are true, different paths to the same goal (the one Reality); they are stages/varieties suited to different temperaments — "as many faiths, so many paths." No religion should destroy another; harmony & acceptance (not mere tolerance). ✅ Advaita ground: since the ultimate is the one non-dual Brahman, all sincere paths (bhakti, jñāna, karma, yoga) converge on it → pluralism is metaphysically grounded, not just pragmatic. ⚠️ Radhakrishnan: religions are diverse interpretations of a common spiritual experience (anubhava) → pluralism.
plain.after: Vedāntic and Vivekanandan pluralism relate many religious paths to one ultimate reality, but the move from shared ultimacy to equal doctrinal truth requires argument.

(2024, 10m) → §9.1 + §9.8 — add Scotus for the contrast. [Pluralism bridge] "How does a theory of religious language bear on religious pluralism?" → §9.10.
answer_line.after: No single theory captures every religious utterance: analogy protects predication, symbol mediates participation, and apophatic language disciplines claims about transcendence.

philosophy-paper-i-indian-philosophy-01.00: Cārvāka is recoverable only through source-critical reconstruction: hostile testimony must be qualified, but convergent reports still establish a stable materialist core.
philosophy-paper-i-indian-philosophy-01.02: Cārvāka attacks inference by arguing that finite observation cannot establish universal concomitance and may always conceal a defeating condition.
philosophy-paper-i-indian-philosophy-01.03: Cārvāka explains consciousness as an emergent property of organised matter, though it offers an analogy of emergence rather than a developed causal mechanism.
philosophy-paper-i-indian-philosophy-01.04: Once perception is the sole independent warrant, soul, creator, rebirth and unseen ritual efficacy lose their claimed epistemic foundation.
philosophy-paper-i-indian-philosophy-01.06: Cārvāka's evidential discipline exposes dogmatism, yet its perception-only criterion is narrower than the reasoning required to defend that discipline.

philosophy-paper-i-indian-philosophy-02.00: Jain realism combines enduring substances with changing modes, making permanence and change complementary aspects of one many-sided reality.
philosophy-paper-i-indian-philosophy-02.01: Jain dharma and adharma are cosmic media enabling motion and rest, not moral merit and demerit.
philosophy-paper-i-indian-philosophy-02.03: Many-sidedness grounds perspectival humility without scepticism, because finite knowledge is partial while perfect knowledge remains possible.

philosophy-paper-i-indian-philosophy-03.02: Dependent origination explains arising through conditions and therefore avoids both eternal substances and causeless annihilation.
philosophy-paper-i-indian-philosophy-03.05: The Buddhist school sequence progressively disputes whether external objects, cognitive representations or any intrinsic nature can count as ultimately real.
philosophy-paper-i-indian-philosophy-03.06: Vaibhāṣika directly perceives external particulars, whereas Sautrāntika infers them from the representations they causally produce.

philosophy-paper-i-indian-philosophy-04.00: Nyāya supplies standards of warranted cognition while Vaiśeṣika supplies a realist ontology, and their synthesis directs true knowledge toward release.
philosophy-paper-i-indian-philosophy-04.01: The seven categories classify independent bearers, dependent features, irreducible relations and absences within a single realist inventory.
philosophy-paper-i-indian-philosophy-04.02: Nyāya defends inference by grounding vyāpti in observation, counterexample control, removal of hidden conditions and hypothetical reasoning.
philosophy-paper-i-indian-philosophy-04.06: New production preserves the novelty of effects, while eternal atoms preserve material continuity through ordered combination.
philosophy-paper-i-indian-philosophy-04.07: A strong Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika answer links realist ontology to pramāṇa method, tests objections fairly and ends with a qualified explanatory verdict.

philosophy-paper-i-indian-philosophy-05.00: Sāṃkhya is a realist dualism of one unconscious material nature and many non-objectifiable conscious witnesses.
philosophy-paper-i-indian-philosophy-05.01: Prakṛti is inferred as the unmanifest common cause whose three-guṇa structure explains the coordinated diversity of mind and world.
philosophy-paper-i-indian-philosophy-05.02: The guṇas are dynamic constituents of prakṛti, not detachable qualities; their changing proportions generate every psychophysical state.

philosophy-paper-ii-philosophy-of-religi.03: Spinoza replaces a purposive creator with one necessary substance from whose nature every finite mode follows.
philosophy-paper-ii-philosophy-of-religi.04: Advaita applies indefinability to māyā and world-appearance, while nirguṇa Brahman remains the non-dual reality beyond limiting predicates.
philosophy-paper-ii-philosophy-of-religi.07: God-models must be compared on common axes of world-relation, human freedom and worship, not by labels considered in isolation.
philosophy-paper-ii-philosophy-of-religi.08: A high-scoring comparison states each model's world-relation, tests its freedom or coherence problem and closes with a named, qualified verdict.

philosophy-paper-ii-philosophy-of-religi.00: Ontological arguments reason from the God-concept, whereas cosmological, teleological and Nyāya arguments begin from experienced features of reality.
philosophy-paper-ii-philosophy-of-religi.02: A cosmological argument succeeds only if contingent or presently dependent reality genuinely requires a non-derivative explanatory ground.
philosophy-paper-ii-philosophy-of-religi.04: Kant's moral argument postulates God and immortality for the highest good; it is practical commitment, not theoretical demonstration.
philosophy-paper-ii-philosophy-of-religi.05: Nyāya infers an omniscient efficient cause that orders eternal atoms and karmic fruits rather than creating matter from nothing.
philosophy-paper-ii-philosophy-of-religi.06: Indian critiques relocate explanatory work to dependent conditions, karma or ritual potency, so they are not reducible to one atheistic objection.

philosophy-paper-ii-philosophy-of-religi.01: Free-will defence establishes possible compatibility between God and moral evil, not a complete explanation of actual suffering.
philosophy-paper-ii-philosophy-of-religi.02: Soul-making gains moral depth from stable natural order, but it risks treating victims' suffering as an instrument for others' development.
philosophy-paper-ii-philosophy-of-religi.03: Augustine denies evil positive substance, while process revisions reduce divine control; each response resolves one pressure by accepting another cost.
philosophy-paper-ii-philosophy-of-religi.05: Indian traditions reshape the evil problem because they disagree about creator, self, karma and the ultimate meaning of liberation.
philosophy-paper-ii-philosophy-of-religi.06: A sound evaluation separates logical from evidential evil, defence from theodicy, and causal explanation from moral justification.
philosophy-paper-ii-philosophy-of-religi.07: A complete answer identifies the challenged divine profile, reconstructs the relevant argument and grants each response only the conclusion it actually establishes.

philosophy-paper-ii-philosophy-of-religi.00: Immortality, rebirth, reincarnation, resurrection and liberation make distinct claims about survival, embodiment and release.
philosophy-paper-ii-philosophy-of-religi.01: Plato's arguments separately support pre-existence, affinity or simplicity and do not automatically establish personal immortality.
philosophy-paper-ii-philosophy-of-religi.03: Buddhist rebirth preserves causal continuity without a permanent self, avoiding both numerical identity and total discontinuity.
philosophy-paper-ii-philosophy-of-religi.04: Liberation terms are not interchangeable, because each presupposes a different self, bondage, method and final state.
philosophy-paper-ii-philosophy-of-religi.05: Knowledge, action and devotion function as alternatives, preparations or integrated paths according to each school's theory of bondage.
philosophy-paper-ii-philosophy-of-religi.06: Resurrection reconstitutes the person after one life, whereas rebirth repeats becoming and reincarnation specifically implies a transmigrating soul.
philosophy-paper-ii-philosophy-of-religi.07: A strong answer defines the survival criterion, compares unlike traditions on common axes and ends with a qualified identity verdict.

philosophy-paper-ii-philosophy-of-religi.00: Reason tests warrant, revelation claims divine disclosure, and faith adds trusting commitment beyond conclusive demonstration.
philosophy-paper-ii-philosophy-of-religi.01: The crucial question is not reason versus faith in the abstract, but which reason assesses which religious claim and with what authority.
philosophy-paper-ii-philosophy-of-religi.02: Revelation claims disclosure unavailable to unaided reason and therefore requires independent tests of authenticity, coherence and moral credibility.
philosophy-paper-ii-philosophy-of-religi.03: Aquinas allows reason to establish preambles of faith while revelation supplies mysteries that exceed, but should not contradict, reason.
philosophy-paper-ii-philosophy-of-religi.04: Kierkegaard locates faith in committed inwardness under objective uncertainty, not in arbitrary belief without reasons.
philosophy-paper-ii-philosophy-of-religi.05: Scientific and religious claims may differ in scope, but miracle and testimony claims still enter ordinary evidential assessment.
philosophy-paper-ii-philosophy-of-religi.06: Religious belief may be inferentially warranted, properly basic or testimony-based, yet every model remains open to defeaters.
philosophy-paper-ii-philosophy-of-religi.07: Faith should be neither reduced to proof nor protected from criticism; it is responsible commitment under incomplete evidence.

philosophy-paper-ii-philosophy-of-religi.00: Religious experience must be analysed through phenomenology, claimed object and epistemic force rather than treated as self-authenticating evidence.
philosophy-paper-ii-philosophy-of-religi.01: James identifies recurrent marks of mystical experience and judges religion by enduring fruits without equating usefulness with truth.
philosophy-paper-ii-philosophy-of-religi.02: Otto's numinous is the non-rational encounter with the Holy as simultaneously overwhelming mystery and attraction.
philosophy-paper-ii-philosophy-of-religi.03: Advaita interprets non-dual awareness as Brahman-realisation, while Radhakrishnan prioritises spiritual intuition over later doctrinal expression.
philosophy-paper-ii-philosophy-of-religi.04: The sacred, the Holy, God and the Absolute are competing object-models, not interchangeable names for one uncontested referent.
philosophy-paper-ii-philosophy-of-religi.05: Perception-like religious experience may have prima facie force, but diversity, pathology and counterevidence can function as defeaters.
philosophy-paper-ii-philosophy-of-religi.06: Prayer addresses the ultimate, worship enacts supreme worth, and public justification must translate private experience into shareable reasons.
philosophy-paper-ii-philosophy-of-religi.07: Public philosophical use of religious experience requires a distinction between sincere testimony, transformative fruit and metaphysical proof.

philosophy-paper-ii-philosophy-of-religi.00: Non-theistic religion is not identical with atheism: absence, irrelevance, denial and suspension of God-belief are distinct positions.
philosophy-paper-ii-philosophy-of-religi.07: Religion without God is conceptually possible where ultimate concern, discipline and transformation survive, though personal providence and theistic worship do not.

philosophy-paper-ii-philosophy-of-religi.00: Religion may ground, reveal, motivate or sanction morality, and these four dependence claims must be assessed separately.
philosophy-paper-ii-philosophy-of-religi.01: Divine command gives obligation authoritative force but faces the dilemma between arbitrary will and independently intelligible goodness.
philosophy-paper-ii-philosophy-of-religi.04: Indian moral grounding ranges from Vedic duty and karma to non-theistic compassion, so dharma cannot be reduced to divine command.
philosophy-paper-ii-philosophy-of-religi.06: Nietzsche exposes life-denying moral genealogies, but his critique must itself answer how power protects equality and the vulnerable.
philosophy-paper-ii-philosophy-of-religi.07: A strong answer separates validity, knowledge, motivation and sanction before comparing theistic and non-theistic moral frameworks.

philosophy-paper-ii-philosophy-of-religi.01: Exclusivism reserves decisive truth, inclusivism recognises others through one fulfilment, and pluralism grants independently valid responses to ultimacy.
